title: The Butterfly Effect
caption: The Butterfly Galaxies NGC 4567 and NGC 4568, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
celestial: Butterfly galaxies · constellation Virgo · about 60 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Two galaxies, NGC4567 and NGC4568, have just begun to collide and merge. Their wing-like outline earned the pair the nickname the Butterfly Galaxies. The pair sits in Virgo, at a distance of around 60 million light-years.

Such collisions are common in the Universe. They sound violent, but the source describes them as surprisingly peaceful, with gravity guiding the stars, gas and dust as they rearrange. Scientists think the Milky Way will one day go through a similar encounter with our neighbor, the Andromeda Galaxy.

The image comes from FORS2, the FOcal Reducer and low dispersion Spectrograph 2, mounted on ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal Observatory in the Chilean Andes. FORS2 is so versatile that it is nicknamed Paranal's Swiss Army knife. As well as taking pictures, it can record spectra of up to several tens of objects at once or study polarized light.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (5.88 x 5.83 arcminutes) and distance (60 million light years), the frame spans roughly 103,000 × 102,000 light-years. Its light set out about 60 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: FORS2 on the Very Large Telescope observed the galaxies in visible light through b, v, R and hydrogen-alpha filters. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
filters: 440 nm · Optical b (Very Large Telescope FORS2)
557 nm · Optical v (Very Large Telescope FORS2)
655 nm · Optical R (Very Large Telescope FORS2)
660 nm · Optical H-alpha (Very Large Telescope FORS2)
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the glow of hydrogen gas, and the telescope's exposures collect far more light than an eye could from such distant galaxies.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The picture was made for the ESO Cosmic Gems program, which uses telescope time that cannot serve science observations to image interesting or visually appealing objects for education and outreach. The data may still be useful for research and are available to astronomers through ESO's science archive.
alt: Two colliding galaxies whose combined outline resembles a pair of wings.
